idiom_name: Map per scope with a parent link (or Object.create(parent) prototype chain), define/lookup functions
implementation_notes: JavaScript gives you the two primitives the pattern needs: Map for the per-scope namespace (average constant-time lookup, any key type, no prototype pollution) and either a plain parent reference or Object.create(parentScopeObject) so that the language's own prototype chain performs the innermost-outward walk. What replaces the classic structure is the built-in Map plus closures - a scope is a small object, define is set with a duplicate check, and lookup is a loop over parent - while the ECMAScript specification's Environment Records (declarative, object, function and global records linked by [[OuterEnv]]) are the formal model of exactly this structure and engines implement it natively (V8's Scope/ScopeInfo pair). Keep the hand-written chain when you build a compiler, interpreter or linter in JavaScript; at runtime you normally do not build one at all, because the engine's lexical environments already shadow correctly.
pitfalls: Plain objects inherit from Object.prototype, so a scope modelled as {} resolves constructor, toString or __proto__ to built-ins instead of reporting an unresolved name - use Map or Object.create(null).
Map compares keys by SameValueZero: identifier strings must be normalised (Unicode escapes in identifiers) before insertion, and interning them avoids growing one map entry per textual occurrence.

A scope captured by a closure is shared by reference: mutating it after a function expression recorded it changes what that function sees (the mutable-environment bug the resolver exists to fix), so snapshot or freeze bindings at capture time.
